plan: Informative essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000037) on Nellie Bly's 1889-90 trip around the world. Topic checked against 36 ACT English passages; every grammar choice set checked against the live bank with chsearch.py (no matches). Skills new to the bank: lead/led, 'off of', 'a number of' agreement, pronoun case after 'between', where/were, past participle 'beaten'; plus goal detail, setup sentence, emphasizing detail (NO CHANGE), conclusion linking to the opening. No transition item.

passages.title: Seventy-Two Days
passages.text:
In 1888, a young reporter for the New York World proposed a stunt: she would travel around the world faster than Phileas Fogg, the hero of Jules Verne's novel Around the World in Eighty Days. Her editors at first {{1|lead}} her to believe that a man would be sent instead, since a woman would supposedly need too much luggage. The reporter, who wrote under the name Nellie Bly, answered that if a man went, she would make the same trip for another newspaper and beat him.

On November 14, 1889, Bly boarded a steamship in New Jersey carrying a single small bag. {{2|}} She crossed the Atlantic to England and continued by train to Amiens, France. When she stepped {{3|off of}} the train there, Verne and his wife were waiting to meet her. Back in New York, the World ran a contest inviting readers to guess the exact length of her trip, and a number of rival newspapers {{4|was}} following her progress.

{{5|Bly continued east across Asia.}} On the day she left, a magazine called Cosmopolitan had sent its own reporter, Elizabeth Bisland, around the world in the opposite direction. The race between Bisland and {{6|she}} drew wide attention, yet for most of the trip neither of the women knew exactly {{7|were}} the other was.

Bly arrived back in New Jersey on January 25, 1890, seventy-two days after she had left. She had {{8|beat}} Fogg's fictional record by eight days, and {{9|thousands of people jammed the station to cheer her}}. {{10|}}

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: her to believe that a man would be sent instead
candidates.explanation: The sentence describes a past action, so the past tense of "lead" is needed: "led."

A.rationale: "Lead" is the present tense (or a metal); the past tense of the verb is "led."

C.rationale: "Leaded" means containing the metal lead and is not a form of the verb.

D.rationale: After "had," the past participle "led" is needed, not "lead."

hints: Is the action past or present?

strategy.explanation: Check the tense of the surrounding verbs.

candidates.remember: Lead (present) / led (past); the metal is also spelled lead.

candidates.subskill: Choosing a detail to fulfill a goal
candidates.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence that emphasizes how lightly Bly packed. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

choices.A: The steamship she boarded was one of the fastest passenger ships crossing the Atlantic at the time.
choices.B: Many reporters and onlookers gathered at the dock to watch the ship leave for England that cold morning.
choices.C: It held little more than toiletries, writing supplies, and a change of underwear; she wore one dress for the entire trip.
choices.D: She had studied train and steamship timetables very carefully for several weeks before she finally left.

candidates.explanation: Only C details how little Bly carried, which emphasizes light packing and answers her editors' worry about luggage.

A.rationale: This is about the ship's speed, not Bly's packing.

B.rationale: This describes the crowd, not how lightly Bly packed.

D.rationale: This describes her planning, not how little she carried.

hints: Which choice is about her luggage?

strategy.explanation: Read the goal before the choices.

candidates.remember: Judge each choice only against the goal in the question.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: the train there, Verne and his wife were waiting
candidates.explanation: In standard written English, "off" alone does the job: "stepped off the train."

A.rationale: "Off of" adds an unnecessary "of"; standard written English uses "off."

B.rationale: "Stepped off to the train" changes the meaning; she was leaving the train.

C.rationale: "Out off" is not a standard phrase.

hints: Does every word in the phrase earn its place?

strategy.explanation: Read the phrase without the extra word.

candidates.remember: Write "off the train," not "off of the train."

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: "A number of" works like "many," so the subject is plural and takes "were." ("The number of," by contrast, is singular.)

A.rationale: "A number of" means "several" and takes a plural verb.

C.rationale: This is singular; "a number of rival newspapers" is plural.

D.rationale: This is singular and present tense; the subject is plural and the events are past.

hints: Does "a number of" mean one thing or several?
candidates.remember: A number of = plural; the number of = singular.

candidates.subskill: Sentence that sets up what follows
candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively sets up the information that follows in the paragraph?

choices.B: Asia was the longest part of Bly's journey.
choices.C: Bly did not know at first that she was in a race.
choices.D: Bly sent regular reports back to her newspaper.

candidates.evidence: had sent its own reporter, Elizabeth Bisland
candidates.explanation: The paragraph reveals a rival reporter racing the other way; saying Bly did not know she was in a race sets up that surprise.

A.rationale: This repeats her route and does not prepare for the news about a rival.

B.rationale: This makes a claim about distance that the paragraph never develops.

D.rationale: Her reports are not what the paragraph goes on to discuss.

hints: What does the rest of the paragraph reveal?

strategy.explanation: Read the paragraph, then choose its opening.

candidates.remember: An opening sentence should prepare for the paragraph's main information.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: Pronouns that follow a preposition such as "between" are objects: "between Bisland and her."

A.rationale: "Between" is a preposition, so its objects take the object case: "her," not "she."

C.rationale: A reflexive pronoun needs an antecedent doing the action in the same clause.

D.rationale: "Hers" is a possessive pronoun and does not fit here.

strategy.explanation: Drop the other name and test the pronoun alone.

candidates.remember: After a preposition, use object pronouns: me, him, her, us, them.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: neither of the women knew exactly
candidates.explanation: The women did not know the other's location, so the sentence needs "where," meaning "in what place."

A.rationale: "Were" is a form of "be"; the sentence needs "where," which refers to a place.

B.rationale: "Wear" means to have on clothing and makes no sense here.

C.rationale: "We're" means "we are," which does not fit.

hints: Is the sentence about a place?

strategy.explanation: Say each choice in the sentence.

candidates.remember: Where = place; were = past of "be"; we're = we are.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: Fogg's fictional record by eight days
candidates.explanation: "Had" forms the past perfect, which takes the past participle: "had beaten."

A.rationale: "Beat" is the base form or simple past; after "had," the past participle is needed.

B.rationale: "Beated" is not a standard form of "beat."

D.rationale: "Had beating" is not a standard verb form.

candidates.remember: Had + past participle: had beaten, had begun, had flown.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively emphasizes the size of the crowd that greeted Bly?

choices.B: some people came to see her arrive
choices.C: there were people at the station
choices.D: a crowd of a certain size gathered

candidates.evidence: Bly arrived back in New Jersey on January 25, 1890
candidates.explanation: Only the original wording ("thousands of people jammed the station") conveys a very large crowd.

C.rationale: This gives no sense of how many people came.

D.rationale: "A certain size" is vague and does not emphasize a large crowd.

hints: Which choice gives a sense of a large number?

strategy.explanation: Read the goal before the choices.

candidates.remember: "Emphasize" calls for the most vivid, specific choice.

candidates.stem: The writer wants to conclude the essay by connecting Bly's success to her editors' doubts described in the first paragraph. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

choices.A: She had circled the globe with one small bag, answering her editors' worry that a woman would need too much luggage.
choices.B: Elizabeth Bisland arrived in New York several days later and went on to write a book about her own journey.
choices.C: Jules Verne's popular novel had first been published about seventeen years before Bly's journey began.
choices.D: Within a few months, another traveler completed the same trip in even less time than Bly had needed.

candidates.evidence: since a woman would supposedly need too much luggage
candidates.explanation: The editors doubted a woman could travel light; A answers that doubt directly by pointing to her single small bag.

B.rationale: This concerns Bisland, not the editors' doubts.

C.rationale: This adds a fact about the novel, not the editors' doubts.

D.rationale: This reports a later record and does not connect to the editors' doubts.

strategy.explanation: Reread the first paragraph, then match.

candidates.remember: When a goal names an earlier detail, the answer must refer back to it.
